lesson.title: Yeast's Escape Hatch: How Alcoholic Fermentation Keeps Glycolysis Running
lesson.summary: When oxygen runs out, yeast and some other microorganisms regenerate NAD+ by converting pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide, letting glycolysis continue to produce ATP without the electron transport chain.
lesson.body:
Glycolysis, the ten reaction pathway that begins glucose breakdown in every living cell, has a hidden requirement that is easy to overlook: it depends on a steady supply of NAD+. In its sixth step, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase strips electrons from glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and hands them to NAD+, producing NADH. If free NAD+ runs out, that step stalls, and glycolysis halts along with the two ATP it nets per glucose. Under aerobic conditions, the electron transport chain reoxidizes NADH back to NAD+ as a side effect of making much larger amounts of ATP. When oxygen is scarce, as it often is for yeast growing deep in a sugary mash, that route is closed. Fermentation is the general name for pathways that solve this problem without oxygen, and alcoholic fermentation is the specific version carried out by yeast and a handful of other microorganisms.

Alcoholic fermentation converts pyruvate, the three carbon end product of glycolysis, into ethanol in two enzymatic steps. First, pyruvate decarboxylase removes a carboxyl group from pyruvate and releases it as carbon dioxide gas, leaving behind the two carbon compound acetaldehyde. This decarboxylation is essentially irreversible under cellular conditions: once that carbon leaves as CO2, the cell has no practical way to reattach it and rebuild pyruvate. This is the key difference from lactic acid fermentation, where lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate directly, without removing any carbon, so lactate can later be converted back to pyruvate when oxygen becomes available again.

Second, alcohol dehydrogenase reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol, and this step actually solves the NAD+ problem: the enzyme pulls electrons from NADH and loads them onto acetaldehyde, regenerating NAD+. That regenerated NAD+ cycles back to the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step of glycolysis, letting glycolysis keep running and keep producing its modest yield of two ATP per glucose by substrate level phosphorylation. Fermentation adds no new ATP generating reactions of its own; its entire contribution is keeping glycolysis unstuck by giving NADH somewhere to unload its electrons.

Saccharomyces cerevisiae, brewer's and baker's yeast, is the textbook organism for this pathway, and its two waste products are used differently depending on the application. In bread dough, the carbon dioxide released by pyruvate decarboxylase gets trapped in the gluten network and forms the bubbles that make bread rise, while most of the ethanol evaporates during baking. In brewing and winemaking, fermentation happens in a sealed or partially sealed vessel where carbon dioxide escapes but ethanol accumulates in the liquid, eventually reaching concentrations high enough to slow or kill the very yeast producing it.

Comparing alcoholic and lactic acid fermentation side by side makes an important point about metabolism: both pathways regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can continue, but they use different enzymes and produce different end products because natural selection found more than one biochemical solution to the same constraint. Neither pathway captures anywhere near the energy that aerobic respiration extracts from the same glucose molecule, since the electrons carried by NADH still hold most of the original bond energy when they are simply dumped onto acetaldehyde or pyruvate instead of passing through an electron transport chain. Fermentation is best understood as a stopgap: a way to keep a little ATP flowing when oxygen is unavailable, at the cost of throwing away most of the energy stored in glucose.
